Patterns of Phone Use in Public Spaces

Introduction

In this visual data story, I will be talking about the phone use observations I have made. By exploring how and who people surround themselves with when using their phone, helps uncover patterns in how technology shapes us. The visualizations aim to provide a brief idea of some common behaviors people interact in when using their phones.

Which Weekday Has the Most Phone Use?

A bar chart showing the number of observations recorded on each day of the week

This plot aims to show which day has the most phone use. As shown in the observations, phone use peaks mid-week (between Tuesday and Thursday), with Tuesday recording the highest number of observations (17). Friday, with the fewest observations (2), indicates that phone use drops off at the end of the week. It is worth noting that no observations were carried out during the weekend. Overall, this visualization shows that mid-week is when phone use is most common, whereas on Monday and Friday, it isn’t.

Comparing How Long Different Phone Activities Last

A column plot showing the average time spent on different phone activities

The second plot shows the time people spend doing certain activities on their phones. The visualization shows that the activity that takes the longest is watching videos. This makes sense as watching a video requires focus which in turn keeps people on their phone longer. Other activities, such as, Scrolling media and Gaming follow close behind as they also tend to take a lot of the focus of its user. Finally, taking photos and typing are the lowest which also makes sense as these activities only require quick interaction behaviors.

Android vs iPhone: Time Spent Using Phones

A box plot comparing time spent on phones between Android and iPhone users

The reason for this plot is to gather an understanding of whether phone type has an impact on duration of phone use. The visualization shows that phone use duration is fairly similar between both phone types. Although there is little variation within each group, the medians are close, further indicating that phone type does not strongly influence how long people use their phones in public.

Conclusion

The graphs highlight clear differences in public phone‑use behaviors, suggesting that individuals engage with their phones in varied ways and that certain activities tend to take more time than others. Additionally, while phone use duration is similar between Android and iPhone users, the greater spread in Android data suggests greater variability in how long Android users engage with their phones in public. Overall, these patterns demonstrate that people use their phones in various ways depending on who they are and what they are doing.
